facts.statement: The genus Voay contains only one known species, Voay robustus.
facts.quote: containing only one species, V. robustus

facts.statement: Voay skulls are noted for having a distinctive pair of horns on the back of the head.
facts.quote: noted for their distinctive pair of horns on the posterior

facts.statement: Fossils of Voay have been found at locations including Ambolisatra and Antsirabe in Madagascar.
facts.quote: from such places as Ambolisatra and Antsirabe

facts.statement: Voay lived during the Late Pleistocene and Holocene epochs.
facts.quote: lived during the Late Pleistocene to Holocene

facts.statement: It is suggested that Voay went extinct around 2000 years ago alongside other endemic megafauna like the elephant bird after humans arrived in Madagascar.
facts.quote: It has been suggested to have disappeared in the extinction event that wiped out much of the endemic megafauna on Madagascar, such as the elephant bird and Malagasy hippo, following the arrival of humans to Madagascar around 2000 years ago

facts.statement: Voay had a shorter and deeper snout and relatively robust limbs compared to the modern Nile crocodile.
facts.quote: It had a shorter and deeper snout than the extant Crocodylus niloticus, as well as relatively robust limbs

facts.statement: Voay robustus measured approximately 3.5 to 4 meters long and weighed about 170 kilograms.
facts.quote: V. robustus would have measured around 3.5 - 4 m long and weighed about 170 kg

facts.statement: A hypothesis that Nile crocodiles migrated to Madagascar only after Voay went extinct was disproved by the discovery of 7,500-year-old Nile crocodile fossils contemporaneous with Voay.
facts.quote: It has recently been proposed that the Nile crocodile only migrated to the island from mainland Africa after V. robustus had become extinct in Madagascar. However, this was subsequently disproved after some Crocodylus specimens from Madagascar were found to be at least 7,500 years old and contemporaneous with Voay

facts.statement: Voay robustus was originally classified in the genus Crocodylus when it was first described in 1872.
facts.quote: When V. robustus was first described in 1872, it was originally assigned to the genus Crocodylus

facts.statement: Voay was assigned to its own new genus in 2007.
facts.quote: it was assigned to the new genus in 2007

facts.statement: A 2021 paleogenomic study identified Voay as a sister group to Crocodylus, with both lineages diverging in the mid-to-late Oligocene.
facts.quote: a 2021 study using paleogenomics found Voay to be a sister group to Crocodylus, with both genera diverging in the mid-late Oligocene
